problem/gpu: Training runs on GPUs, short for graphics processing units: chips first built to draw graphics, which do thousands of multiplications at once. Each has only so much memory.
problem/copy: Data parallelism gives every GPU a full copy of the weights, w, and its own slice of the batch.
problem/big: But the biggest models have more weights than one GPU can hold: not even one copy fits.
problem/cut: So cut the model itself into pieces, one per GPU: inside each layer's matrix, or between the layers.
columns/x: Take one layer. Its input, x, is a list of numbers; call its length d. Here d is two, and x is one and two.
columns/W: Big models usually write the layer with x on the left, times the weights, W one: one row per input, and one column per output.
columns/wide: This layer widens to four times d outputs, so W one is d by four d: here, two by four.
columns/cols: Each output is x dotted with one column. Output zero: one times one, plus two times one: three.
columns/split: So cut W one between its columns: GPU zero keeps columns zero and one, and GPU one keeps columns two and three.
columns/own: Each GPU computes its own outputs: three and two on GPU zero, two and one on GPU one. The ReLU works entry by entry, so each applies it to its own part.
columns/shape: With k GPUs, the columns are shared k ways: each GPU's piece is d by four d over k.
rows/w2: The next matrix, W two, is four d by d: it takes the four d values back down to d. Cut it by rows to match: GPU zero gets the two rows that read its own outputs.
rows/rshape: With k GPUs, each piece is four d over k, by d.
rows/part: Now each GPU's product is only part of the answer: three and two on GPU zero, one and two on GPU one. These are partial sums.
rows/sum: Add them across the GPUs for the real output: four and four. That exchange happens inside every layer, every step, so this split needs very fast links between GPUs.
rows/megatron: Mohammad Shoeybi and colleagues at NVIDIA split their models this way in 2019, in Megatron-LM, and trained a model of eight point three billion parameters across five hundred and twelve GPUs.
rows/tensor: Tensor is the word for any array of numbers, such as a vector or a matrix. Cutting the weight matrices themselves is called tensor parallelism.
pipeline/layers: Or cut between whole layers. Twenty four layers on four GPUs: six consecutive layers each, called a stage.
pipeline/which: Counting from zero, stage zero holds layers zero to five, so layer thirteen lands on stage two: thirteen over six, rounded down.
pipeline/send: Each stage hands its output to the next, and during backprop, the gradient on that output comes back. Nothing else crosses.
pipeline/gpipe: But one batch at a time keeps only one stage busy. In 2018, Yanping Huang and colleagues at Google fixed that in GPipe: cut the batch into micro-batches, and feed them in one after another.
pipeline/name: While stage one works on the first, stage zero starts the second, like an assembly line. That flow is a pipeline, hence pipeline parallelism.
pipeline/compare: So the column split talks inside every layer, the layer split only at its cuts, and data parallelism once per step.
